sections.content: How many people stayed in Worksop after gaining qualifications?

Worksop is a medium-sized town in the East Midlands. Worksop does not have its own university.

Worksop has higher levels of deprivation.

Overall, Worksop ended up with:

  • fewer graduates than it produced
  • fewer non-graduates with advanced qualifications than it produced
Note: all towns and cities in this analysis are defined based on population size only. This means that some cities are classed as towns because of their population.

Let's explore this further

There were 2,115 state-school pupils from Worksop who sat their GCSEs between the 2007 to 2008 and the 2010 to 2011 school years.

Of these, 520 (25%) went on to gain degree-level qualifications (level 6+ as defined by The Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulation, or Ofqual ). We will call these people graduates.

Another 585 (28%) went on to gain other advanced post-16 qualifications, such as A-Levels, a foundation degree or higher apprenticeship (levels 3-5 as defined by Ofqual). In this tool, we will refer to these non-graduates with advanced qualifications as “qualified non-graduates", for brevity.

The charts below compare Worksop to other English towns and cities using three measures:

  • what proportion of Worksop's pupils became graduates or qualified non-graduates by the 2017 to 2018 academic year
  • of those graduates and qualified non-graduates, the percentages that lived in Worksop in the 2018 to 2019 academic year
  • how many graduates and qualified non-graduates from elsewhere came to live there by 2018 to 2019, relative to the number who sat their GCSEs there

In some towns, some of this information may not be available because of small sample sizes.
The size and deprivation level of a town, as well as the qualification levels of older residents, were all related to students' educational attainment. Read our previous analysis.

Where did those who left Worksop move to?

Of Worksop's graduates, 210 were living elsewhere in 2018/19.

However, 25 of those graduates (12%) were living fairly locally, in the Worksop and Retford travel to work area (TTWA).

Of Worksop's qualified (level 3+) non-graduates, 160 were living elsewhere in 2018/19.

However, 65 of those qualified non-graduates (41%) were living fairly locally, in the Worksop and Retford travel to work area (TTWA).

Of those in Worksop's GCSE cohort:

  • 150 graduates left the East Midlands
  • the most common region they moved to was Yorkshire and The Humber
  • 65 qualified (level 3+) non-graduates left the East Midlands
  • the most common region they moved to was Yorkshire and The Humber

In 2018 to 2019, 18% of graduates and 20% of qualified non-graduates living in Worksop had moved there from elsewhere

In the 2018 to 2019 academic year, there were 370 graduates and 520 qualified (level 3+) non-graduates from our cohort living in Worksop. This is compared with the 520 graduates and 585 qualified non-graduates who had lived there when they sat their GCSEs.

In 2018 to 2019, 82% of the graduates had also lived in Worksop as GCSE pupils, while 18% had moved there from elsewhere.

Of the qualified non-graduates who lived in Worksop in 2018 to 2019, 80% had lived there as GCSE pupils, while 20% had moved to the area from elsewhere.
